Although the three types of multivibrators function slightly different, the troubleshooting procedures are very similar.
DISCUSSION
Let's look at an astable multivibrator and develop some simple troubleshooting steps.
When Vcc is applied to a normal operating astable multivibrator, two out of phase square waves should be present at points D and E.
Usually, an interruption anywhere in the multivibrator results in either no output at point E and Vcc at point D or vice versa.
Since many different faults could cause the same symptoms, a basic troubleshooting method is needed.
Once you have measured the circuit outputs and determined that they are incorrect, measure Vcc at point A to ensure that the supply voltage is correct.
If Vcc checks good, the next step is to check the transistors. These components are more likely to fail than any of the others.

Troubleshooting a monostable multivibrator is not much different than troubleshooting an astable multivibrator.
Monostable multivibrators change extremely short input pulses into long output pulses.
The two outputs are always opposite. The trigger causes one output to go high for a certain length of time and the other to go low for that same time.
Checking the input trigger, Vcc, both transistors, and making resistance measurements will determine the faulted component..
These same procedures can be used to troubleshoot bistable multivibrators.
A trigger input causes the outputs to change states until the next trigger is applied.
After determining the output is faulted ensure that the trigger pulse is present.
Use this troubleshooting method as a guide to help you troubleshoot multivibrator circuits.
This is not the only method, and you may develop your own techniques as you become a more proficient troubleshooter.
